Maladaptive Strategies.value: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied
go over and over why the event happened to me
I dwell on how I used to be before the event

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

vignette:
At 76 years old, Margaret had seen many storms in her life, both on the open sea and within her own heart. As a ship captain, she had navigated rough waters, led her crew through challenging times, and battled the elements. But nothing compared to the turmoil that had engulfed her since the day police violence disrupted her life. It was a warm summer evening when she had ventured into town, a routine trip to replenish supplies for her vessel, a trip that had turned into a nightmare. 

Margaret remembered the sounds of laughter and chatter in the market, the smell of fresh bread wafting through the air, so different from the salty breeze she was accustomed to. She had been in line at the bakery, her hands resting on the counter, when a sudden commotion erupted outside. Her heart raced as she caught sight of the commotion—a young man being forcibly restrained by officers. The memory was vivid, etched in her mind like a photograph. She recalled the shouts, the chaos, and the sight of the young man struggling against the officers. In that moment, she felt a gut-wrenching fear unlike any other, as if the violence was happening to her. 

Since that day, Margaret had found herself throwing herself into her work, a habit that had grown more pronounced as time passed. The ocean became her refuge, yet even there, she could not escape the haunting images that replayed in her mind like a broken record. She would sit at her desk in the captain's cabin, poring over navigation charts and maintenance logs, willing herself to focus on the tasks at hand. The sea was vast and unyielding, just as her thoughts had become. She often found herself ruminating on the event, wondering why it had happened to her, why she had witnessed such brutality when her only intention had been to enjoy a simple day. The questions circled like gulls above her head, relentless and consuming.

It was during quiet moments alone on the boat that Margaret's thoughts would drift back to the past. She would dwell on how life had been before that fateful day—the camaraderie of her crew, the thrill of steering her ship through uncharted waters—and she longed for the simplicity of those days. The memories felt like a distant shore, always out of reach, and she often found herself weeping for the life she once knew, a life unmarred by the trauma she had endured.

As the months turned into a year, Margaret's symptoms intensified. The vividness of her memories became almost unbearable; it felt like she was reliving the event each time it crossed her mind. She could see every detail—the anger on the officers' faces, the fear in the young man's eyes, the chaos of the moment. Sometimes, when she was alone, she could hear the shouts and the crack of a baton striking against flesh as if she were right there again. These recollections filled her with dread, and she started to avoid the townspeople, fearful of encountering anyone who might remind her of that day.

The isolation crept in slowly, a shadow that enveloped her life. Margaret began to decline social invitations, missing gatherings with her fellow captains, fearing that a simple discussion about the sea would spiral into something more personal, something she wasn't ready to confront. As her relationships began to fray, she felt the weight of loneliness settle heavily on her shoulders. 

It was during one of those long nights spent staring at the stars above her boat that Margaret finally acknowledged the depth of her suffering. She could no longer ignore the fact that her work, once a source of pride and joy, had transformed into a means of escape. The fear that had taken root in her heart was growing, and she could sense that she was losing herself to the memories she could not bear to face. 

What frightened her most was the thought that she might never feel whole again, that the vibrant woman who had danced with the wind and waves might be lost forever to the darkness that had seeped into her life. It was this realization that brought her to seek help, a flicker of hope amidst the storm. Margaret wanted to reclaim her joy and restore the connections she had let slip away. She longed for guidance, a way to navigate through the treacherous waters of her mind and find a safe harbor once more.
